blocks.md: **Across US commuting zones ordered by 1970 population density, four things changed between 1970 and 2015: dense places became far more educated; they lost middle-skill jobs much faster; for non-college workers, those jobs were replaced by low-skill service jobs; and the urban wage premium shrank for the least educated but not for the most educated.**
All values read off the lecture charts, approximate. Each point is a group of commuting zones holding about 3–5% of the working-age population.

sections.heading: I. Bigger cities became much more educated

blocks.src: assets/Attachments/US college and dropout shares by city density 1970-2015.png
blocks.alt: US college and dropout shares by city density 1970-2015

blocks.md: The college gradient across density steepened sharply.

sections.heading: II. Bigger cities lost middle-class jobs much more rapidly

blocks.src: assets/Attachments/US occupational employment shares by city density 1970-2015.png
blocks.alt: US occupational employment shares by city density 1970-2015

blocks.md: Employment shares relative to the 1970 mean: middle-skill jobs (production, clerical, admin, sales) in the densest zones fell from ≈ +0.05 (1970) to ≈ −0.19 (2015); in the least dense they barely moved (≈ −0.12 to −0.15). High-skill jobs rose most in dense places (≈ +0.04 to ≈ +0.23).

blocks.src: assets/Attachments/US non-college occupational shares by city density 1970-2015.png
blocks.alt: US non-college occupational shares by city density 1970-2015

blocks.md: For **non-college** adults, dense places swapped middle-skill jobs for low-skill ones (services, transport, construction, laborers): the low-skill share in the densest zones rose from ≈ −0.08 to ≈ +0.15, while non-college high-skill shares barely changed.

sections.heading: III. Bigger cities lost their wage advantage for the least educated

blocks.src: assets/Attachments/US log hourly wages by education and city density 1970-2015.png
blocks.alt: US log hourly wages by education and city density 1970-2015

blocks.md: In 1970 log hourly wages rose with density for every education group. By 2015 the gradient had flattened for workers without a high-school degree and steepened for post-college workers.

- These are cross-sectional patterns by 1970 density, not causal effects.
- The occupation shifts are the spatial face of [Wage Polarization](note:wage-polarization): middle-skill jobs vanished fastest exactly where they were most concentrated.
- They motivate regional analysis: something interesting happens across space, beyond its usefulness for identification.
